title: Baseline Behavior
description: A person's normal, resting state of behavior when they are comfortable and unthreatened.

sections.title: Quick Understanding
sections.content: A baseline is strictly how someone acts when they are under fundamentally zero stress. You cannot accurately formally identify if a behavior is a 'stress signal' or a 'lie' unless you absolutely first establish what that exact person looks and sounds like when they are totally relaxed.

sections.title: What It Looks Like
content: Their completely normal rate of speech and speaking volume.
Their standard, comfortable amount of eye contact.
Their typical everyday use of hand gestures.
Their default resting posture and neutral facial expression.

sections.title: What It May Indicate
content: Understanding the baseline is the essential calibration phase of observation. It tells you their true default setting.
Massive, sudden deviations from this baseline dynamically indicate a massive shift in emotion or an extreme spike in cognitive load.

sections.title: What It Does NOT Mean
content: A rapidly nervous baseline does NOT mean they are always chronically lying. Some people are just totally naturally anxious.
A perfectly calm baseline does NOT magically guarantee honesty. Some people are naturally profoundly low-arousal or heavily practiced at deception.

sections.title: Real Life Examples
content: Interrogation: Asking extremely basic background questions (name, address, hobbies) to intensely see how the suspect normally sits and speaks before suddenly asking about the crime.
Negotiation: Doing casual, easy small talk safely before the meeting starts to deeply gauge the other party's relaxed posture.
Relationships: Knowing that your partner normally taps their foot aggressively when watching TV, so foot-tapping isn't a sign of explosive anger for them specifically.

sections.title: Cluster Analysis
content: Baseline (relaxed, lots of hand gestures) -> Sudden shift (rigid posture, hands totally frozen) = Severe spike in cognitive load or sheer fear.
Baseline (fast talker, low eye contact) -> Sudden shift (slow deliberate speech, highly intense staring) = Desperately overcompensating to actively sound truthful.

sections.title: Common Situations
content: The absolute first five minutes of any interview or high-stakes negotiation.
Meeting someone intimately for the very first time.
Starting a highly difficult confrontational conversation with a partner.

sections.title: Observation Mistakes
sections.content: Mistake: Actively analyzing someone's nonverbal behavior without firmly baselining them first. Reality: If you incorrectly assume someone utterly avoiding eye contact is lying, but their actual baseline is just extreme, chronic social anxiety, you have failed the most basic fundamental rule of observation.

sections.title: Practical Observation Tips
content: Spend the exact first few minutes of a major interaction asking harmless, trivially easy questions ('How was your weekend?') solely to watch their body.
Carefully note how much they naturally naturally blink and wildly move their hands.

sections.title: Red Flags
content: An immediate, totally drastic shift completely away from the baseline (e.g., normally very highly talkative, but going totally morbidly silent and rigid as soon as a topic is merely raised).
Absolutely refusing to safely establish a baseline (giving extremely hostile one-word answers to basic social pleasantries).

sections.title: Reality Check
sections.content: Perfectly baselining takes time and immense situational awareness. It is not a magical 5-second TV process. Furthermore, environmental factors (like a literally cold room or a highly recent argument) can temporarily significantly alter a person's baseline.
